reading.body:
Construction AI is measured, not guessed: Census BTOS surveys firms fortnightly, AGC tracks contractor adoption, and BuiltWorlds plus proptech trackers follow the tools, with computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning as the working deployments.

The pattern is narrow and physical. The named deployments all watch the jobsite or check a digital model against reality before concrete is poured, so the value is in catching discrepancies early, not in generating designs or schedules. That makes construction AI an on-site perception and verification problem, where the binding constraints are accurate site data and timely action before work proceeds.

What the data does not show is how widely these tools are used, what they save, or how often they fail. It establishes that adoption is tracked through a federal survey, a trade body, a research network, and venture flow, but those sources still reflect firms and startups that choose to report, not the entire industry.

summary: Computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning are the working deployments - the sector's AI mostly watches the jobsite and checks the model against reality before concrete is poured.

analysis.body:
The most direct measure of AI use in construction comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Construction (NAICS 23), the latest figure is 15.4%, down from 16.0% in the prior period. That is the only quantified adoption number in this material, and it describes recent use by firms rather than plans or pilots.

What the sector's own intelligence network shows is where the attention is going. BuiltWorlds, which runs member research and benchmarking across construction technology, hosts an annual AI/ML Conference on artificial intelligence and machine learning in the AEC/O industry, covering existing and emerging solutions and use cases across the construction, building, and operation process, strategies for implementation at the project and enterprise levels, and case studies with lessons learned. Its Buildings Conference focuses on innovation in development, design, materials, and systems, with a specific emphasis on data centers and AI infrastructure. A 2026 conference session is framed around founders showcasing AI's practical power in construction.

The trade body's role is narrower in this material. The Associated General Contractors of America, with over 27,000 member firms, is described as surveying technology adoption and safety-technology compliance across US builders, making its data the adoption record for the trade. The excerpt from its page itself covers member services and a safety conference rather than AI findings, so no AGC adoption figures appear here.

Money and vendors concentrate around events and networks rather than disclosed deal values. CREtech New York 2026 is described as a real estate AI conference expecting 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and 20,000+ pre-scheduled 1:1 meetings at the Javits Center, with sessions led by operators actively deploying AI across their portfolios and speakers drawn from owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction companies, brokers, and technology leaders. CREtech and MetaProp are cited as tracking venture flow across architecture, engineering, and construction technology alongside property tech, though no investment totals are given in this material.

On returns, the sources offer case studies and implementation experience rather than measured ROI. BuiltWorlds describes conference content on how companies are utilizing specific solutions and the lessons learned, and CREtech describes operators sharing real strategy from CIOs, CEOs, and managing directors deploying AI across real assets. Neither reports a quantified return, and the material does not include regulatory posture or risk findings for construction specifically.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a modest reading. The Census Bureau's 15.4% shows a minority of construction firms using AI in any two-week window, and the direction from the prior period is slightly down. The practical knowledge being assembled, per BuiltWorlds and CREtech, is about use cases, project and enterprise implementation, and lessons from companies that have already deployed. The sources here do not provide cost, ROI, or compliance guidance, so those questions remain open on this evidence.

https://cretech.com/.brief: According to the page, CREtech New York 2026 will be held at the Javits Center in New York City on October 20, 21, 2026, and will bring together 3,000 leaders, 150 speakers, and more than 20,000 pre-scheduled 1:1 meetings. The event is described as a leading real-estate AI conference where sessions are led by operators actively deploying AI in their portfolios, offering real strategy rather than theory. The conference aims to connect owners, developers, investors, occupiers, construction firms, brokers, and tech leaders to discuss AI’s impact on real-estate assets. Tickets are limited, and sponsors and partners are said to represent companies shaping the future of real-estate in the age of AI.

https://www.agc.org/.brief: The Associated General Contractors of America describes itself as serving more than 27,000 member firms, offering a range of services intended to address members' needs and concerns. According to the organisation, those services aim to improve the quality of construction and to protect the public interest. The page also promotes an event in San Diego that it says brings together construction safety professionals from around the country to share ideas, build relationships, and take proven solutions back to their teams.

https://builtworlds.com/.brief: BuiltWorlds operates a membership network for buildings and infrastructure professionals. The organization hosts an annual Buildings Conference addressing innovation in building development, design, materials and systems, with particular focus on data centers and AI infrastructure. It also runs an annual AI/ML Conference exploring artificial intelligence and machine learning adoption across the architecture, engineering, construction and operations industry, covering implementation strategies, use cases, and lessons learned from companies deploying these technologies.
